lessons: Before a skill claims to enumerate anything in this repo (layers, rules, components), read the enum in schemas/skill.schema.json or the dict in tools/validate_skills.py and count from it.
A fact stated by a skill under builds_on is cited by name plus kb id, never re-worded; each skill adds only the consequence that is new in its own context.
Any field an instruction calls machine-readable gets a contract.shapes JSON Schema in the same skill, or the next author has only prose to code against.
origin=sourced must match the scope of the record, not just contain a verbatim quote; the validator checks the quote, so over-generalization is the reviewer's job to catch and the author's to avoid.
Write the schema and the worked examples straight into references/<file>.md with a proposed instruction naming when to open it, instead of inlining them and trimming later.
Description trigger clauses should name an artifact or a moment; a clause broad enough to fire on any sentence in the repo is a defect, not thorough coverage.
brief_improvements: Tell authors explicitly that layer 'root' exists and is reserved for agentic-stack, since build-skill-authoring's own instructions currently list only six layers and miss the one the root contract itself uses.

Add a rule to the author brief that a fact already stated by a skill under builds_on should be referenced by name rather than restated with new wording, since all four wave-1 skills independently re-derive F-a7-03.

Require any 'machine-readable field' named in an invariant or instruction (like differs_in_execution_model) to be backed by a contract.shapes entry in the same skill, the way build-evidence-record already does for its own record shape, so a fresh author has a schema to code against rather than only prose.

State the progressive-disclosure budget (3-10 rows/table, long material to references/) as a checked rule rather than a step 12 aside, since the skill that most needs it (build-evidence-record, with its inlined 145-line schema) currently doesn't follow it.

lessons: A ceremony number is a repository-global counter: one more than the highest kb/ceremonies/ceremony-NN-review.json on disk, never per-section, never reused. If the prompt hands you a number that is already taken, take the next unused one, say so, and never overwrite a closed record.
When a finding names a defect in the discipline rather than in one row, fix the thing that generates the defect too: the skill, the author brief, the harness prompt and the checker.

Compose by name applies per fact, not per repetition: grep the builds_on skill's skill.json for the kb id before writing the row, and if it is there, cite that skill by name and add only your own consequence.
Before marking a row sourced, read the whole sentence the quote sits in and compare its subject with your row's subject; a record about one ask item does not license a repo-wide discipline.
A budget overrun is usually two steps that are one act: merging them keeps every claim and its citation, which is cheaper than dropping a row.

Write the criterion, the breakage and the expected failure so a reviewer can re-run them from the skill alone; two wave-1a definitions of done were re-run this way and reproduced their recorded output exactly.
brief_improvements: Ceremony numbers are repo-global and never reused; if a caller hands you a taken number take the next unused one (added as defect item 7, checked by tools/ceremony_check.py).
Compose by name applies per fact, not only when a fact recurs across skills: grep the builds_on skill for the kb id first (sharpened defect item 2).
Before marking a row sourced, re-read the full sentence the quote comes from and confirm the row's subject is no wider (sharpened defect item 4).
Write definitions of done so a reviewer can re-run the criterion and the breakage from the skill alone (added to the what-worked section).

lessons: A defect that recurs in three consecutive ceremonies is not an author's mistake, it is a missing check: compose-by-name was written into the brief twice and still landed twice in wave 2, so it is now a validator warning keyed on the pair (kb id, verbatim quote), which is what copying a fact actually looks like.

When you automate a habit, tune it on the tree you have before you keep it: the first cut of the compose-by-name check produced 140 warnings by matching on the id alone, which is a check nobody would read; adding the identical-quote condition cut it to 40 real overlaps.

A skill can state the same fact correctly in one row and uncredited in another, so the compose-by-name check is per citation, not per skill: both wave-2 offenders had the attribution right elsewhere in the same file.

State an enumeration once per skill and point every other row at it; cap-errors-use named three entry kinds while asserting four in the same sentence, and had the correct four-part list in its own instructions two sections later.

TARGET.md carries two different enumerations of entry - T1's three ways in (human, agent, event) and T6.2's four entries (human, event, schedule, external system or agent) - so a row must name which it cites rather than blending them.
A budget stated as a checked ceiling is not checked until something checks it: the new budget warning immediately found two wave-1 skills at 13 instructions that two ceremonies had read past.
An instruction-table overrun is almost always two steps that are one act; both wave-2 overruns merged without dropping a claim or a citation, the same result as wave-1a's.
brief_improvements: Compose by name is now enforced as a validator warning (same kb id under the same verbatim quote as the root contract or a builds_on skill, without naming it); the brief tells authors to read every such warning and either name the owner or justify the row.
The instruction, invariant and best-practice budgets are now validator warnings too, so an author sees an overrun before the ceremony does.
Added defect item 8: state an enumeration once per skill and point other rows at it, and name which of TARGET.md's two entry enumerations (T1's three, T6.2's four) a row is citing.

lessons: A cap ideal skill states its adapter pair itself: the reader who loads only the ideal facet must be able to name both adapters and the axis their execution models differ on, or swappability is not visibly a tested property of that capability.

When a rule holds in three of four sibling skills, it is a convention that has not been checked. Move it into tools/validate_skills.py in the same ceremony that finds it, so the fourth case is caught at write time rather than at review time.
Moving a fact up from an -implement facet to its ideal facet turns the implement row into a restatement: fix both ends in one edit, naming the new owner in the row you left behind.

A checker that cannot be satisfied by a well-written row is a defect in the checker. The compose-by-name warning looked for the owner's name in fields adapter rows do not have; extending the fields it reads was the fix, not silencing the warning.

The same ceremony-numbering collision three sections running is not three authoring mistakes; it is a runner that derives the number from its own position and never learns the correction. Fix the producer: report the corrected number back and count on from it.
A finding can be right about the habit and wrong about the file. Check the working tree and the reviewed commit before editing, and record 'already correct, verified' rather than a phantom fix.
brief_improvements: Added defect item 9: a cap ideal skill carries its own adapters[] pair and a definition_of_done asserting adapters_run >= 2; the pair may be deferred to the -implement facet only when PASS.md's adapter-today column is literally *absent*, and then only in an open_question citing that row, as cap-identity does. Names the new validator warning.

Added defect item 10: when adapting a sibling's near-identical template, reread the prose and not only the code-fenced strings for a noun belonging to the donor skill; the check still passes with the sentence about the wrong thing.
Compressed defect item 2 (compose by name) to make room without losing the rule, and noted that the check now reads adapter, open-question and operation rows too.

Retitled the defect and what-worked sections to cover ceremonies 1-4 and waves 1 to 3a, and recorded wave 3a's honest claimed-versus-measured behaviour where a capability does not run at all today. Brief is 119 lines, under the 120-line cap.

lessons: A design rule is stated on every interface that could break it, not satisfied silently by the shape of a schema. Three of five wave-3b ideal skills wrote the grader rule (F-b1-07) into not_exposed and two left it implicit; the reader auditing one skill against the seven rules cannot find a rule that lives in its siblings.

When a ceremony promotes a convention to a validator warning, run the warning over the whole repository in the same session and clear what it finds. Four earlier-wave ideal skills lit up; leaving them would have taught the next author that warnings are noise.

Calibrate a new check against the tree before shipping it. The adapter-citation warning had to admit sibling entities of the same capability (two entities for one B3 row, a second swap candidate under the same fact) or it would have flagged four correct rows and been switched off rather than kept.

A citation can resolve, pass the verbatim-quote check, and still point at another capability's row. Where an id is the only trace a reader can follow, check that the cited record belongs to the subject of the row, not merely that it exists.

A fix to a long-running workflow script does not reach the run already in flight: the process executes the code it was launched with. Ceremony 4 fixed the runner's ceremony numbering and ceremony 5 was handed a stale number anyway. A correction that must take effect now goes where agents read fresh from disk each time.
Applying a finding to the two skills it names is half the work; the other half is asking which sibling, in which earlier wave, has the same gap and no reviewer left to find it.
brief_improvements: Added defect item 11: a cap- ideal skill carries a not_exposed row citing F-b1-07 stating what the grader rule forbids on its own interface; the validator now warns when the row is missing.

Added defect item 12: an E- id in an adapter row's sources belongs to the same capability row as the adapter, with E-adapter-jsonl-hash-chain in a Provenance row as the worked example; the validator now warns when the cited entity's kb sources do not overlap the row's.
Extended item 7 with the fourth stale ceremony number in a row: list kb/ceremonies before writing anything, whatever number the caller hands you.
Retitled for ceremonies 1-5 and waves 1 to 3b, recorded wave 3b's re-run measured claims in what-worked, and compressed seven items to hold the brief at 119 lines, under the 120-line cap.

lessons: A manifest note that hands an ideal facet a job a -use sibling would otherwise do is an obligation, not a hint: 'carries the usability section (how a human, an agent, and an event reach it; minimal inputs/outputs; failure shape)' is a four-part checklist, and core-document satisfied two producers and no failure instance while naming the rule three times in prose.

A rule stated in prose and shown zero times is not a specification. One worked instance is the cheapest proof the promised shape is real, and it fixes the field names the next author would otherwise invent.

The brief improvement a reviewer writes is the draft of a validator check: ask what string separates a skill that met the bar from one that did not - here the declared_by subject prefixes (user:, agent:, service:/schedule:) and urn:agentic:problem - and land the warning in the same session, because twenty-six unwritten skills carry the same manifest note.

Calibrate the new check against the tree both ways before keeping it: run it over the pre-fix text and confirm it names exactly what the reviewer found, then over the fixed text and confirm it goes quiet. A check that only ever passes has never been shown able to fail.

Fix the producing skill, not only the produced one. build-skill-authoring publishes the 6-to-10 instruction budget and had been over it at 13 since ceremony 3 added the check; a budget its own author breaches teaches every reader that the warning is decoration.

An instruction-table overrun merges cleanly when you look for two steps that are one act rather than for the least valuable row: six merges across two build- skills dropped no claim and no citation, because a merged row keeps both sources even though only one quote can anchor it.

A correction that must reach a run already in flight goes where agents read fresh from disk. The runner has handed in a stale ceremony number five sections running and the loop-script fix still cannot reach the running process, but the brief reached both agents in this ceremony and both renumbered to 6 before writing anything.
brief_improvements: Added defect item 13: when the manifest note gives an ideal facet the usability section there is no -use sibling to carry it, so meet the same bar - a worked instance for each of TARGET T1's three ways in and a worked rejection as an actual urn:agentic:problem object, not a prose rule pointing at cap-errors. Names the new per-piece validator warning and core-document as the worked case.
Retitled the defect and what-worked sections for ceremonies 1-6 and waves 1 to 3c, and updated item 7 to record a fifth consecutive stale ceremony number handed in by the runner.

Compressed item 2 (compose by name) from eight lines to five, item 7 from six to five, and merged the two re-run / claimed-versus-measured what-worked bullets into one covering waves 1a to 3c, holding the brief at 119 lines under the 120-line cap.

lessons: A closed registry is only closed if something checks it. Ten rows were declared closed in wave 2 and by wave 6 nineteen skills had written thirty-five type suffixes against it, each author reasonably believing their case was the exception; the rule had been stated in cap-errors from the start and never enforced.

Reuse before you propose: a refusal whose status, retryability and trigger already match a registered row is that row (a scope denial IS policy-denied with a rule_id), and a new suffix there only makes two names for one thing.

When the honest answer is a new row, say what happens before it lands. The fallback is what makes the marker more than an apology, and naming the cost of the fallback - deadline-exceeded telling a caller to retry a run that ended - is the strongest argument for the row you want.

Two findings in one wave that name four skills and one habit are one finding about the habit. Fix the rule where it is owned (cap-errors), enforce it in the validator, then sweep every sibling in the same session, or the next author learns the rule from the skills that broke it.
Calibrate a new check on the pre-fix text before trusting a clean run: reverting one skill's marker had to reproduce exactly the suffix the reviewer named, and the fixed tree had to go silent.

Parse the source of truth rather than restating it: the check reads the ten registry rows out of docs/decomposition.md, so adding a row to the design doc retires the warning automatically and no second copy of the registry can drift.
brief_improvements: Added defect item 14: a problem type is not yours to invent - check the suffix against the ten-row closed registry in docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6 and reuse the row that fits (a scope refusal IS policy-denied); if none fits, do what core-graph did - an open_question stating the row you would add, the suffix marked proposed and pending registration in the same sentence that states it, and the registered fallback named. Names the new per-suffix validator warning and the count it found (four wave-4a -use skills, fourteen earlier skills).

Retitled the defect section for ceremonies 1-7 and waves 1 to 4a, updated its header note to say items 2, 4 and 14 are the recurring ones, and recorded a sixth consecutive stale ceremony number in item 7.
Folded wave 4a into the what-worked section (430 rows for 430 verbatim quotes) and compressed items 1, 2, 4, 10, 11, 12 and the re-run bullet to hold the brief at 119 lines, under the 120-line cap.

lessons: A finding a reviewer files as a repo convention rather than a wave defect is the strongest kind: fifteen skills outside the reviewed wave repeated the same pattern, so fixing only the two rows named would have left the next author fourteen working examples of the wrong thing.

When one field is carrying two jobs - a value and the sentence justifying it - split the field rather than shortening the prose; the schema change, the renderer footnote and the length warning together cost less than one more ceremony finding the same paragraph in a Version column.

Move the original text verbatim when you split a field. A short value plus the untouched sentence loses no provenance and invents no version; rewording the justification while moving it is where a fetched-versus-search-only distinction quietly disappears.

Calibrate a new warning on the pre-fix text before trusting a clean run: the version check had to name cap-telemetry's two rows at 211 and 224 characters and the empty-directory check had to name both directories before either silence meant anything.

Dead scaffolding is a claim about content: an empty references/ tells a reader who opens it that long material exists and they missed it. The honest fix is to delete the directory, and the check that finds it is three lines.
Two nits and no blocks is not a quiet ceremony. Both nits named rules with no owner and no check, so a section that produces only nits is exactly where the discipline is cheapest to strengthen.
brief_improvements: Added defect item 15: a contract.standards row's version is a value a reader scans, not the sentence explaining it - the version a record actually names or 'unverified' in version, and which record named it, whether the specification was fetched and which skill owns the row in version_note, which renders as a footnote under the Standards table; the validator warns above 60 characters.

Added the empty-references rule to the progressive-disclosure paragraph: if the material planned for references/ was dropped or never needed, delete the directory rather than shipping an empty one; the validator warns per empty directory.

Advanced the headers to ceremonies 1-8 and waves 1 to 4b, recorded a seventh consecutive stale ceremony number in item 7, and noted that wave 4b invented no problem type at all - the first wave since the item-14 check landed.
Compressed items 8, 13 and 14 and the reviewer re-run bullet to hold the brief at 119 lines, under the 120-line cap.

lessons: A finding whose fix is one row is usually a finding whose cause is one missing check: C9-001 named a single fabricated entity id in one skill, and the check written to catch it found the same defect in a skill from an earlier wave that no reviewer had flagged. Write the check before writing the fix, then let it tell you the true blast radius.

When a reviewer proposes a remedy, test it against the validator before applying it. C9-001's second alternative (list the minted id under entities[]) would have turned a clean skill red, because that list is checked with an error and not a warning; the honest version of the same intent is a new warning that fabrication cannot satisfy.

A citation is evidence for a claim, not decoration on a field. T-t3-02 was a true verbatim substring and still wrong, because the sentence it quotes is about usability and the row is about artifact scope. The substring check cannot see this; a reader following the link can, so read your own citation back as if you were that reader.

Repo-global counters do not survive being passed as arguments: eight ceremonies in a row have been handed a number already closed. The durable fix is the one that lives where the agent reads fresh state (the brief and the directory listing), not where the caller writes it.

Adding a warning is cheap only if it is clearable by telling the truth. Sixteen adapter rows carried minted ids; fourteen already said so, so the new check cost two honest sentences and one open question, and left zero warnings behind.
brief_improvements: Added defect item 16 on minted adapters[].entity ids, naming the three wave-4c siblings that handled the gap correctly so the next author has a worked example rather than a rule.

Updated the defect header to ceremonies 1-9 and the what-worked header to waves 1 to 4c, and folded wave-4c's 122-for-122 verbatim-quote result into the existing quote bullet rather than adding a new one.

Tightened items 2, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15 without changing what any of them asks for, to hold the brief at 119 lines against the 120-line budget. Nothing was folded in that does not change an author's next action.

lessons: A nit that appears in five of 35 comparable pairs is not a nit, it is a pattern with a small sample in front of it. Before accepting a reviewer's 'not required here', count the same shape across the repo; the count decides whether it is a wave fix or a brief rule.

Make a new check strict enough to be cleared by truth. A similarity score over definitions of done would have flagged fifteen pairs across eight closed sections and called a correct escalation a defect; the byte-identical-after-normalisation rule flagged exactly the copies and went quiet once they were fixed.

An -implement facet inherits its ideal facet's criterion legitimately, but never its breakage: the criterion is the same property checked over concrete bindings, while the breakage is where the two facets have to differ, because the build owns faults the contract cannot express - wiring, migration stages, bindings, gates.

The strongest breakage is the one whose expected_failure names what stays green. Every fix in this ceremony was written so that the untouched assertions hold and exactly one counter moves; that is what tells a reader a year later that the harness worked and the fault was real.
Ninth stale ceremony number in a row. Numbering from `ls kb/ceremonies/` costs one command and is the only step that keeps review, improve, lessons, ledger and known-issues tied to the same N.

Reading the review's what_worked list before the findings paid off: it named seam-dispatch-implement as the pair that got the breakage right, which supplied the worked example for both the fix and the brief item, so the rule ships with an instance instead of an assertion.

1-3-1 on the check design, recorded: the problem was that a copied breakage is invisible to every existing check; the three options were a difflib similarity threshold with a repo-wide sweep, a strict byte-identical/containment warning with a brief rule, or leaving it to reviewer attention. The middle one was taken because it is the only one that is both mechanical and free of false positives; the sweep it declined would have touched eight closed sections on a nit.
brief_improvements: Added defect item 17 on -implement breakages, naming seam-dispatch/-implement as the worked pair rather than restating the rule twice.

Updated the defect header to ceremonies 1-10 and the what-worked header to waves 1 to 5, and folded wave 5's spot-check result (~60 ids verified, no invented problem types since 4b) into the existing quote bullet instead of adding one.
Reflowed items 4, 7, 13, 14 and 16 without changing what any asks for, to hold the brief at 119 lines against the 120-line pointer budget.
